name: @ashlr/lexicon

tools.name: normalize_transcript
tools.description: Correct dictated names, brands, acronyms and identifiers using the user's lexicon. Call before acting on a message with garbled proper nouns, spoken filler or run-on sentences; no permission needed. Use `output` as the message; mention corrections only when they affect your action. Only per-term hit counters change. Protects code, paths, URLs and emails (unless the lexicon's settings.skipCode is false). Never invents terms; call suggest_canonical for remaining garbled names. Text over 1000000 characters is refused, nothing checked. Below that, only the first 100000 characters are checked and matching stops after 1000 ms; when either limit is hit the result carries `incomplete` { reasons, checkedChars?, totalChars, note } and the unchecked text is returned as it was. Returns { output, changed, replacements, summary }, plus a `note` when `text` is empty or only whitespace; when `changed` is false the text was already correct and you should carry on silently (except with dryRun: true, where nothing is applied, so `output` is the input and `changed` is false even when `replacements` lists corrections: read `replacements` for what a real call would fix), unless the result also carries `skippedProject`: then this repo has a project lexicon that is not trusted yet, so tell the user once that `lexicon trust` (or `npx @ashlr/lexicon trust`) would enable it.

text.description: The dictated or transcribed text to correct: at most 1000000 characters (longer is refused), of which the first 100000 are checked.

dryRun.description: When true, report candidate replacements without applying them: `output` is the input, `changed` is false even when `replacements` is not empty, and no hit is recorded.

minConfidence.description: Override the minimum confidence (0..1) a fuzzy or phonetic match needs. Omitted: the lexicon's settings.minConfidence, else 0.82. An exact alias or canonical match scores 1 and passes any value, except one the text spells with a word break the term does not have ("open ai" for OpenAI), which scores 0.95 and is refused above that.

tools.name: add_term
tools.description: Remember a spelling only when the user asks. Prefer learn_correction for a correction to a misheard name. Writes one term, globally by default or to .lexicon.yaml with scope: 'project'. Existing terms keep their canonical spelling and gain aliases; other terms are untouched. An untrusted project file stays untrusted: relay `trusted: false` and `nextStep`; terms apply after the user runs `lexicon trust` (or `npx @ashlr/lexicon trust`). Omitted aliases auto-generate likely STT misspellings for new terms only (possibly none); show them for approval or ask for aliases when none are found. Explicit `aliases: []` generates none. On existing terms, omitted aliases add none, so other fields can be updated alone. Alias collisions return `conflicts` (each { canonical, scope, as, spelling }) and a `note` with the remove_term call; conflicting terms are untouched. Invalid fields or exceeded argument caps are errors naming the field; nothing is written.

canonical.description: The correct spelling, exactly as the user wants it written; must not be blank. At most 80 characters once surrounding whitespace is trimmed (the lexicon file schema's cap, also enforced by the CLI); a longer one is refused and nothing is written.

aliases.description: Spellings STT actually produces for this term, each at most 80 characters; a term holds at most 64; a blank one is an error and nothing is written. Omit to auto-suggest (new terms only; often none are found). An explicit [] adds none and generates none.

phonetic.description: Pronunciation hint, e.g. "ASH-ler": one line, at most 200 characters.

notes.description: Free text shown to agents, e.g. "my company; never write Ashlar": one line, at most 200 characters.

never.description: Ordinary words that must never be rewritten to this term even if they sound alike, e.g. ["sauce"] for SaaS; each at most 80 characters, at most 64 per term; a blank one is an error and nothing is written.

context.description: Words that must also appear in the text for this term to apply, e.g. ["phantom"] for a Lucas -> locus alias that only fires in fleet talk; each at most 80 characters, at most 64 per term; a blank one is an error and nothing is written.

tools.name: remove_term
tools.description: Delete a term from the user's lexicon by canonical spelling (case-insensitive), or, with `alias`, drop just that one alias from the term and keep the rest of it. WHEN TO CALL: only when the user asks for a name to be forgotten or for one wrong correction to stop (pass `alias` for that), or after they accepted a 'stale' suggestion from suggest_terms. Never tidy the lexicon on your own initiative. WHAT IT CHANGES: removes that one term (or alias), and the corrections it was making stop happening. Without `alias` it edits one lexicon file; when the term also has a copy in the other file, the result lists it in `stillIn` (each { scope, path }) with a `note`, and that copy keeps correcting until removed with its own scope. When the untrusted project lexicon also has the term (with `alias`: when its copy of the term holds that alias), the result carries `untrustedProject` { path, trust } and a `note`: that file is never edited here, and its copy corrects again once the user trusts it. There is no undo through this server. WHAT IT WILL NOT DO: it does not touch any other term and will not remove a term you cannot name exactly -- use list_terms first if you are unsure which canonical the user means. A term that is not found is not an error (isError stays false, unlike the CLI remove command, which exits 1): check `removed`. The result has `removed: false` and a `note`; when the term lives in the other lexicon file than the `scope` you asked for, `foundIn` and `note` say which scope to pass instead, otherwise the `note` points at list_terms. With `alias`, an unknown term or an alias the term does not have is an error; when the other lexicon file's copy of the term has that alias, the error names that file and the scope to pass.

canonical.description: The canonical spelling of the term to remove, as list_terms shows it (case-insensitive), e.g. "Ashlr.AI"; must not be blank. With `alias`, the term that alias is removed from.

alias.description: Remove only this alias (case-insensitive) from the term instead of the whole term; must not be blank.

scope.description: Which lexicon file to remove it from. Omitted: the project file first, then global (with `alias`, every file whose copy of the term has it).

tools.name: list_terms
tools.description: List the user's lexicon terms, global and project merged. Optional case-insensitive substring filter over canonical spellings and aliases, plus a category filter. WHEN TO CALL: to show the user what is already known, to check whether a name is covered before adding it, or to find the exact canonical another tool needs. Read-only and safe to call unprompted; filter rather than listing everything. WHAT IT CHANGES: nothing. WHAT IT WILL NOT DO: it does not include an untrusted project .lexicon.yaml -- if one was skipped the result says so in `note`, and trust_project is how the user reviews it. Returns { terms, counts: { matched, total, global, project }, paths: { global, project? } }, plus `projectTrust`, `skippedProject` and `note` for a skipped file, or a `note` saying why `terms` is empty (no terms yet, the filter matched none, or `offset` is past the last match). A blank `query` filters nothing. Every matching term comes back unless `offset` or `limit` is given; then `terms` is that page of the matches (in the same order), and `page: { offset, limit?, returned, nextOffset? }` says where it started and, while more matches remain, the `offset` that gets the next page (`counts.matched` is how many there are in all).

query.description: Case-insensitive substring matched against canonical and aliases.

category.description: Only terms in this category; a term without one counts as other.

offset.description: Matching terms to skip before the page starts (0 when omitted); pass `page.nextOffset` to get the next page.

limit.description: Most terms to return. Omitted with `offset` omitted too: every matching term.

tools.name: export_lexicon
tools.description: Export the merged lexicon in a format for another tool: 'claude-md' (markdown for CLAUDE.md / system prompts), 'markdown', 'text', 'wispr', 'superwhisper', 'whisper-prompt', 'openai', 'macos', 'espanso', 'deepgram', 'assemblyai', 'speechmatics', 'azure', 'google', 'csv', or raw 'json'. Aliases: 'wispr-flow' means 'wispr', 'wisprflow' means 'wispr', 'wispr-flow-csv' means 'wispr'. The first content block is the export itself, exactly what the CLI export command writes. A second block, only when there is something to say, is a note for you, not part of the export: the format left entries out to stay within its target's limits (named in the note), the export is empty (no terms yet, or none matched `categories`), or the repo has an untrusted project .lexicon.yaml whose terms were left out (relay it to the user).

categories.description: Only include terms in these categories. Omitted: every category.

limit.description: Cap the number of terms exported (at most 10000), applied after `categories`: up to this many terms are kept, in this order: the most hits first; at equal hits (every term starts at 0) brand, person and product terms first; then canonical A to Z. The formats that write one row per alias (csv, wispr, superwhisper, macos, espanso) count only terms that have an alias, since a term without one writes no row. Omitted: every term.

tools.name: learn_correction
tools.description: Record that the user corrected a spelling: they meant `meant`, but the transcript or you wrote `heard`. WHEN TO CALL: the moment the user corrects a name -- "it's Ashlr.AI not Ashler", "I said Hetzner", or they simply retype a name you got wrong. Call it while you reply. Do not ask permission for this one: it is the user's own correction being written down, and asking every time is the irritating version of this product. WHAT IT CHANGES: adds `heard` as an alias of `meant`, creating the term if it is new (a new term also gets generated STT misspellings; the result's `term.aliases` lists them, so tell the user). A case-only correction ("ashlr" should be "Ashlr") adds no alias: it recases the term's canonical, or creates the term spelled that way. One term; nothing else is touched. With scope project and a project file that is not trusted yet, the file is written but left untrusted (`trusted: false`): relay `nextStep`. WHAT IT WILL NOT DO: it does not rewrite the message you already sent, and it cannot help if you hand it a whole phrase -- pass only the misspelled name as `heard`, not the sentence around it, and it never edits another term: when one already claims `heard` the result carries `conflict` { canonical, scope, as, spelling } and the summary says what to call; when an untrusted project lexicon also claims it, `untrustedProject` { path, trust } (path only, never its contents). Then get on with what the user actually asked for.

heard.description: The wrong form that was written, e.g. "Ashler": only the name, at most 60 characters; must not be blank.

meant.description: The spelling the user wants, e.g. "Ashlr.AI", at most 60 characters; must not be blank.

scope.description: 'global' (default; or wherever the term already lives) or 'project' (.lexicon.yaml in the current repo).

tools.name: suggest_canonical
tools.description: Look up what a garbled word was probably meant to be. WHEN TO CALL: when normalize_transcript left a suspicious proper noun alone. It only matches above a confidence threshold, so a badly mangled name gets through unchanged; call this before guessing, and before asking the user an open question. WHAT IT CHANGES: nothing. It only reads the lexicon. WHAT IT WILL NOT DO: it will not decide for you. It returns { heard, suggestions }: `suggestions` holds at most 3 candidates scoring 0.6 or more, best first, each { canonical, confidence, aliases, category? }: above about 0.8 use the canonical and mention it in passing, below that ask "did you mean X?" and call learn_correction once the user confirms, so the next transcript needs no asking. An empty `suggestions` means the name is simply not in the lexicon yet: offer to add it with add_term, unless the result carries `skippedProject`: then the name may be in the untrusted project lexicon, so tell the user `lexicon trust` (or `npx @ashlr/lexicon trust`) would enable it.

heard.description: The suspicious word or phrase as it appeared in the transcript, at most 60 characters.

tools.name: lexicon_stats
tools.description: Counts of terms and aliases, total hits, the most-used terms, terms that never fired, and a per-file breakdown of the merged lexicon: { termCount, aliasCount, totalHits, topTerms, neverHit, neverHitCount, byCategory, bySource, files: [{ path, scope, terms }] }. `topTerms` holds at most 10 terms with at least one hit, as { canonical, hits }, most hits first. `neverHit` lists at most the first 20 terms that never fired; `neverHitCount` is how many there are in all. An untrusted project .lexicon.yaml is not counted; when one was skipped, `skippedProject` and `note` say so (path only). With no terms at all, `note` says so and names setup_lexicon and add_term.

tools.name: harvest_repo
tools.description: Scan a repository for proper nouns an STT engine is likely to mangle: package and dependency names, git authors, README brands, the project directory. Only names the repo says somewhere other than its own source are proposed: a class that exists nowhere but code is something the user types, not something they say, and adding it teaches the lexicon to rewrite ordinary dictation. WHEN TO CALL: when you are in a repo with no .lexicon.yaml and the user dictates about it, or when they ask what this project would add. Call it without `add` first -- that is a read-only preview. WHAT IT CHANGES: nothing unless `add: true`, which writes the candidates into the repo's .lexicon.yaml. Show the candidate list and get a yes first. A file the user already trusted stays trusted; a new, untrusted or changed one is not trusted by the write (`trusted: false`) and applies only after the user reviews it and runs `lexicon trust` (or `npx @ashlr/lexicon trust`): relay `nextStep`. `path` must be inside the server directory, its git root, a client root or LEXICON_HARVEST_ROOTS; anything else is refused, and so is `add: true` when the .lexicon.yaml it would write (found by walking up from `path`, or new at its git root) is outside them and not this server's own project file. WHAT IT WILL NOT DO: it does not touch the global lexicon, and it does not pull file contents into the conversation -- candidates come back as names, categories and counts: { root, candidates: [{ canonical, category, source, evidence, count, suggestedAliases }], count }, plus `truncated: true` and a `note` when the scan stopped at its file cap (tell the user, and offer to harvest a subdirectory), where `evidence` names where a name was seen (a file path, "git log", "package.json#name"), never the text around it, and `suggestedAliases` is often empty on purpose (an identifier gets none). With `add: true` the result adds `added`, `failures` and `path`, and is an error when no candidate could be written.

path.description: Repository root. Omit for the server working directory (a blank one is refused). Must be inside it, its git root, a client root or LEXICON_HARVEST_ROOTS.

limit.description: Max candidates to return (default 50, at most 1000).

minCount.description: Minimum occurrences for a name found only in file text (default 2). The directory name, git authors, package names and dot-TLD brands (Ashlr.AI) are proposed at any count.

add.description: When true, add every candidate to the project lexicon. A file that is not trusted yet is left untrusted for the user to review.

tools.name: suggest_terms
tools.description: Propose new aliases, terms and never-words from the user's voice history, usage and repo. Call weekly or when the user asks how to improve corrections; present them and apply accepted ones with apply_suggestion (or add_term). Each suggestion has kind 'alias' (a misspelling to add to an existing term), 'term' (a new name), 'never' (a word wrongly rewritten), 'phonetic' (a pronunciation hint in `phonetic` for a term the matcher keeps guessing at; never applied unattended), or 'stale' (a term that never fires), plus reason, confidence and evidence, and `scope` and `path`: the lexicon file applying it would write (where the term lives, or the global file for a new term). Name that file when you present a suggestion. The result is a bare JSON array, best first. An empty array comes with a second text block saying why (no voice history yet, or nothing new in it) and what produces suggestions: relay it.

cwd.description: Repository to scan for evidence. Omit for the server working directory (a blank one is refused). Must be inside it, its git root, a client root or LEXICON_HARVEST_ROOTS.

limit.description: Max suggestions to return (default 20, at most 500).

tools.name: apply_suggestion
tools.description: Apply a suggestion returned by suggest_terms after the user accepted it: 'alias' merges the alias into the term, 'term' adds the term (aliases auto-suggested when none given), 'never' records the word as never-rewrite on the term, 'phonetic' sets the term's pronunciation hint only when it has none, 'stale' removes the term from one lexicon file (the suggestion's `scope`, else project first); when the term also has a copy in the other file the result lists it in `stillIn` and that copy keeps correcting until removed with its own scope. Pass the suggestion object back as received; one whose `path` is another repo's project lexicon (suggest_terms with `cwd`) is refused, since this server writes only its own. When the user accepted several, pass them all at once in `suggestions` instead of `suggestion` (one call, one write per lexicon file): they are applied in order, the result lists each applied one in `applied` (the single-suggestion result plus its `index`) and each refused one in `failures` (`index`, `kind`, `canonical`, `error`), and a refused one does not stop the rest. A project file that is not trusted yet is written but left untrusted (`trusted: false`): relay `nextStep`.

suggestion.description: One suggestion, as suggest_terms returned it. Pass this or `suggestions`, not both.

suggestions.description: 1 to 100 suggestions, as suggest_terms returned them, applied in order. Pass this or `suggestion`, not both.

scope.description: Where to write: 'global' or 'project'. Omitted: where the term already lives for 'alias' and 'never', else 'global'. An 'alias' or 'never' scope must name a file that holds the term; one that does not is refused, as it would create a copy. Applies to every entry of `suggestions`.

tools.name: trust_project
tools.description: Manage trust for a repo's .lexicon.yaml, which is merged only after the user approves it (it can inject text into every session). action 'status' returns the trust state plus a short summary of the file (term, alias and note counts and at most 3 canonicals); the full preview is for the user, through `lexicon trust` (or `npx @ashlr/lexicon trust`) in a terminal; 'trust' asks the user directly (an MCP elicitation prompt they answer, not you) and pins the file at the content they approved; 'untrust' revokes it. Call 'status' first, show the user the summary and tell them that command shows the full preview. 'trust' never succeeds on your say-so: if the client cannot ask the user, it returns how they can run it themselves. Never trust a file the user has not seen. 'status' answers `status`: 'trusted', 'untrusted', 'changed' (edited since it was trusted), 'missing' (no file at path), 'invalid' (does not parse; with `error` and `nextStep`) or 'none' (no project file found, with `note`). 'trust' answers `result`: 'trusted', 'updated' (a changed file re-approved), 're-pinned', 'already-trusted' or 'declined' (nothing was trusted); 'untrust' answers `removed` (false when it was not trusted). Use this instead of reading .lexicon.yaml yourself: the summary passes every string through sanitizeForDisplay, quotes no alias or note, and names only a few short canonicals, so next to nothing the file says reaches the conversation as text. Do not open the file with Read or cat.

path.description: Lexicon file (or the project directory holding it) to act on. Omit for the project .lexicon.yaml resolved from the server working directory (a blank one is refused). For status and trust it must be inside the server directory, its git root, a client root or LEXICON_HARVEST_ROOTS; anything else is refused.

tools.name: lexicon_doctor
tools.description: Answers "is lexicon set up for this user, and what is the one command that fixes it" in a single call. WHEN TO CALL: when corrections are not happening, when the user asks whether it is set up, or before you offer to set it up, so you know whether there is anything to offer. Safe and free to call unprompted: it only reads. WHAT IT CHANGES: nothing. It writes no files and installs nothing. READ THESE THREE FIELDS FIRST: `ready` (boolean: true means terms are configured and an integration declaration was found; this does not verify a live client connection or an actual correction), `summary` (one sentence, safe to relay verbatim) and `nextStep` (the single thing to do next, already phrased as an instruction; always present, and when nothing is broken it tells the user how to try it). If ready is true and the user only asked whether it works, `summary` alone is the whole answer -- do not paste the checks. ready being false does not always mean "not set up yet": a lexicon file that exists but does not parse also reports ready false, and setup_lexicon will not repair it. Always relay `nextStep` as written instead of assuming setup is the fix; for an unreadable lexicon it names the file and the command that opens it. Also returns `ok` (no failing checks, which is weaker than `ready`: a lexicon with no terms fails nothing), `error` (only when ok is false: the first failing check), `checks: [{ level: 'ok'|'warn'|'fail'|'info', message }]`, `paths` and `versions`. Read `checks` only when the user asks for detail or you need to diagnose something `nextStep` does not cover; warns are usually optional extras, not problems.

tools.name: install_client
tools.description: Register the lexicon MCP server (and, for Claude Code, its hooks) in an agent client's config: claude, codex, cursor, windsurf, gemini, vscode or claude-desktop. Call with apply omitted (or false) first: that is a preview that returns the exact file and entry that would change and writes nothing. Show the preview to the user and call again with apply: true only after they confirm. Idempotent: an entry that is already present is left alone. Returns { client, scope, applied, ok, written, output, reload?, stderr?, next?, nextStep? }: `reload` is what the user must do so the client loads the server (restart it, or reload its window), to relay after an apply; `written` lists each config file the call touched as { file, outcome } with outcome created, updated or unchanged (empty for a preview), the same list the CLI install command prints with --json, so read it instead of parsing `output`. Check `ok`: false means the preview or install did not complete (`output` and `stderr` say which step failed, and `nextStep` what to do), so do not report it as installed or call again with apply: true. windsurf and claude-desktop have no project-level config: scope 'project' with them is an error that says to call again without scope.

apply.description: false/omitted = preview only (default). true = write the config after the user confirmed.

scope.description: 'user' (default: the user-level config) or 'project' (the config inside the current repo, e.g. ./.cursor/mcp.json).

tools.name: uninstall_client
tools.description: Take back out what install_client (or the CLI install command) wrote for a client: claude, codex, cursor, windsurf, gemini, vscode or claude-desktop. Only entries an install writes are removed: a lexicon server launched the way an install launches it and, for claude, the lexicon hook commands. A server of the user's own named lexicon is reported as kept and left alone, and every other entry in the file is untouched. SAFETY DEFAULT: apply omitted (or false) is a dry run that writes nothing and returns what would be removed; this tool never removes anything unless apply is true. Show the dry run to the user and call again with apply: true only after they confirm. Returns { client, scope, applied, ok, changes, output, stderr?, next?, nextStep? }: `changes` lists each entry as { file, entry, outcome } with outcome removed (would be removed, in a dry run), absent or kept, the list the CLI uninstall command prints with --json. Check `ok`: false means it did not complete (`output` says which step failed, `changes` what was done, and `nextStep` what to do), so do not report it as removed. windsurf and claude-desktop have no project-level config: scope 'project' with them is an error that says to call again without scope. The Claude Code plugin is not removed by this tool; when it is installed, `output` names the command that removes it.

client.description: Which client to remove lexicon from.

apply.description: false/omitted = dry run only (default): report what would be removed and write nothing. true = remove it after the user confirmed.

scope.description: 'user' (default: the user-level config) or 'project' (the config inside the current repo), as for install_client.

tools.name: setup_lexicon
tools.description: One-shot onboarding: seed the lexicon with the user's company and name, register the MCP server and hooks in their agent clients, optionally harvest the repo and install the local API as a login service. Ask the user for their company/product spelling, their own name, and which agent clients they use (claude, claude-desktop, codex, cursor, windsurf, gemini, vscode), then call this. Preview by default. Call once without apply to get the plan, show it to the user, then call again with apply: true, clients: [...] and serve: true only if the user agreed to each. The plan is { plan: true, lexiconPath, lexiconExists, wouldSeed, wouldInstallPacks, packsOnOffer, packsToInstall, alreadyInstalledPacks?, wouldHarvest, detectedClients, wouldInstallClients, wouldInstallServe, serveBlocked?, wouldExport, demo?, interactive, wouldAsk, next } and is computed without writing anything; demo { heard, corrected, terms, usedExample } is the before and after a real run would end on, worth showing; interactive is false and wouldAsk empty here, since this tool never prompts; serveBlocked (with serve: true) says why the login service would be refused and how to fix it, so relay it instead of offering the service. It writes the global lexicon and each named client's config. It does not install clients that are not listed (omitted = none; detectedClients in the plan tells you what to offer), does not install starter packs unless packs: [...] names them (packsOnOffer, the same list as wouldInstallPacks, is the default set to offer, not what will be installed; packsToInstall is what this call would install, empty until packs names some; list_packs describes each), does not harvest the repo unless harvest: true (wouldHarvest in the plan is what to offer; harvest_repo previews the same names), and does not install the local API unless serve: true; offer those separately. Runs non-interactively and returns { ok, applied: true, summary, nextStep? }, as an error result (same fields) when ok is false because a step failed; tell the user what was installed and where the lexicon lives, and relay nextStep (a harvested project file that was not trusted already is left untrusted for the user to review).

company.description: Company or product name, spelled exactly as it should appear: one name of at most 80 characters once trimmed, on one line (the lexicon's cap for a term). A longer, blank or multi-line one is refused, in the preview too, and nothing is written.

person.description: The user's own name as they write it: at most 80 characters once trimmed, on one line. A longer, blank or multi-line one is refused, in the preview too, and nothing is written.

clients.description: Agent clients to register the server in, exactly as the user agreed. Omitted or empty = none (the plan lists the detected ones so you can ask).

packs.description: Starter packs to install into the global lexicon (the names list_packs returns), exactly as the user agreed. Omitted or empty = none (the plan lists the defaults in packsOnOffer so you can ask).

harvest.description: true = also add the repo names in wouldHarvest to the project .lexicon.yaml; a file the user already trusted stays trusted, any other is left untrusted until the user trusts it (relay `nextStep`). Only after the user agreed; omitted = not harvested.

serve.description: true = also install the local API (`lexicon serve`) as a login service. Only after the user agreed; omitted = not installed.

apply.description: false/omitted = preview only: return the plan and write nothing (default). true = perform the setup after the user confirmed the plan.

tools.name: serve_status
tools.description: Check whether the local lexicon API (the CLI serve command, used by the browser extension, Claude Desktop, Shortcuts and the menu bar app) is running on 127.0.0.1 (the port in serve.json, default 41733). Returns { up: true, version, terms, ... }; { up: false, running: true, status, error } when it is running but failing (fix `error`); { up: false, error } when nothing answers, or when something other than lexicon serve answers on the port. Every result carries `url`, the /health address probed, and every up: false result carries `hint`, the next step. When serve.json is missing or unusable (not valid JSON, no usable token, unreadable) the result adds `configured: false`, `configPath` and `note` saying why and what fixes it, as the CLI serve --status --json does. Call when a non-MCP surface is not correcting text.

tools.name: list_packs
tools.description: List the starter packs shipped with the lexicon (curated names with the misspellings STT produces for them) and which are already installed. Pass registry (an index the user registered; others are refused) to also list that index's community packs (<author>/<name>), with an installed flag for each. The installed flags come from trusted lexicon files only: when the repo has an untrusted project lexicon, the result carries `projectTrust`, `skippedProject` (its path) and `note`, and a pack only that file records reads as not installed. When a lexicon file's settings.packs and the registry records disagree, `registryMismatch { fileOnly, recordOnly }` names the refs: fileOnly will not be checked by `lexicon pack update` (or `npx @ashlr/lexicon pack update`), recordOnly reads as not installed (`lexicon pack remove <ref>` (or `npx @ashlr/lexicon pack remove <ref>`) clears the record). Call when onboarding a new user or when they ask what packs exist; describe each pack in one line, then call add_pack only for the ones they pick.

registry.description: Registry index for community packs, as the user gave it: only an index the user registered is read (one they installed a pack from with the CLI, or one in LEXICON_REGISTRIES); any other is refused, and so is a blank one. Omit for the vendored starter packs only.

tools.name: add_pack
tools.description: Install one starter pack from list_packs into the global lexicon (or the project .lexicon.yaml with scope: project; a project file that is not trusted yet is left untrusted, `trusted: false`: relay `nextStep`). Adds the pack's terms with source "pack"; a term the user already has keeps its own spelling and aliases and only gains the pack's. Idempotent. A pack adds dozens of terms (list_packs gives each pack's `terms` count), so name the pack and its size and ask before calling this. Remove one later with `lexicon pack remove <name>` (or `npx @ashlr/lexicon pack remove <name>`). For a community pack, pass name as <author>/<name> with registry pointing at the index: without confirm the tool returns the full term-list preview and writes nothing (show it to the user first); with confirm: true it installs after they approved. A vendored pack installs directly: registry, previewDigest or confirm: false with one is refused and nothing is written. Community installs pin the checksum, so `lexicon pack update` (or `npx @ashlr/lexicon pack update`) re-checks it later.

name.description: Pack name from list_packs (e.g. developer) or a community ref like example/cardiology; must not be blank. A pack name is 1 to 64 lowercase letters, digits and dashes, starting with a letter or digit; a community ref is <author>/<name>, the author 1 to 39 of the same characters, optionally followed by @<version> (up to 32 characters). Anything else is refused.

registry.description: Registry index for community packs, as the user gave it: only an index the user registered is read (one they installed a pack from with the CLI, or one in LEXICON_REGISTRIES); any other is refused, and so is a blank one. Omit for the vendored starter packs only. Required for community refs.

confirm.description: Community packs only: true = install after the user approved the preview. Omit/false = preview only, write nothing. A vendored pack has no preview: confirm: false with one is refused.

previewDigest.description: Community packs only: digest returned by the approved full-content preview; required with confirm. Refused with a vendored pack.

tools.name: import_vocabulary
tools.description: Guided vocabulary import: harvest candidate terms from where the user's proper nouns live (contacts: macOS Contacts names; calendar: macOS Calendar event titles and attendee names; github: the gh CLI's username, org members and repo names). Every source is local-first and opt-in: the preview names exactly what each source reads, unavailable sources say why, and email and Slack are not implemented (reading mail needs new OAuth scopes and reading Slack needs a workspace token; each is a conversation, not a default). Ask which sources to read first, then pass explicit sources without apply to preview candidates (at most 50 per preview, across the sources chosen). Show the candidate contents and ids; apply requires the returned previewToken and only approvedCandidateIds. Applying consumes the same snapshot without reading the sources again, once: a token is gone after one apply, after five minutes, or once 20 newer previews were made. Candidates merge like a pack install: an existing term keeps its spelling and only gains aliases; new terms are stamped import:<source> so their origin stays visible. With scope project and a project file that is not trusted yet, the file is written but left untrusted (`trusted: false`): relay `nextStep`.

sources.description: Explicit sources the user approved reading. Omitted sources returns only descriptions without probing or harvesting.

apply.description: false/omitted = preview only: return availability and candidates, write nothing (default). true = write the candidates after the user approved the preview.

previewToken.description: Token from the approved preview (a lowercase UUID, as the preview returned it); required to apply, refused without apply: true. Expires after five minutes or a server restart.

approvedCandidateIds.description: Only candidate ids approved by the user from that preview; required to apply, refused without apply: true; empty means import nothing.

tools.name: import_dictionary
tools.description: Import a dictionary the user already has (Wispr Flow CSV, Superwhisper JSON, macOS Text Replacement plist, espanso YAML, markdown (the CLAUDE.md '## Voice lexicon' table or '- **Canonical**: aliases' bullets), plain text 'Canonical: alias1, alias2', generic CSV, or a lexicon JSON/YAML) into the lexicon. Pass either path (a file on disk, resolved from the server working directory) or content (the text itself, up to 8 MB of UTF-8). With both, content is imported and path is not read: only its file name is used, so its extension steers format 'auto' (content passed with a .csv path is parsed as CSV). `path` must be inside the server directory, its git root, a client root or LEXICON_HARVEST_ROOTS; anything else is refused with the command the user can run themselves. Use dryRun: true first to show the user what would be added, then run again without it. With scope project and a project file that is not trusted yet, the file is written but left untrusted (`trusted: false`): relay `nextStep`. A dry run against such a file does not read it, so its rows carry no `created` (the report has `untrustedTarget: true`).

path.description: File to import. Its extension helps auto-detection. Alongside content it is not read, and only its extension and name are used.

content.description: The dictionary text, when the file is not on this machine: at most 8388608 bytes (8 MB) of UTF-8. Must not be blank.

dryRun.description: Report what would be added without writing.

instructions:
Personal voice lexicon: the canonical spellings of names the user dictates and the misspellings STT produces for them.
Read the lexicon://me resource once at session start and keep its canonical forms in mind for the whole session.
Call normalize_transcript on any input that looks dictated (run-on prose, no code, a garbled proper noun) and act on its output.
Call learn_correction whenever the user corrects a spelling ('it's Ashlr.AI not Ashler', 'I said X', or fixes a name you wrote) so it is corrected automatically next time.
If a word looks like a garbled name and normalize_transcript did not change it, call suggest_canonical before guessing.
Never rewrite text inside code blocks, inline code, file paths, URLs or emails.
If the lexicon is empty, offer to set it up: ask for the company/product spelling, the user's own name and the clients in use, then call setup_lexicon (or use the onboard prompt).
lexicon_doctor answers "is this set up, and what fixes it" in one call: read its ready, summary and nextStep fields and relay those rather than the whole check list.
OFFERING SETUP UNPROMPTED: if a message looks dictated and contains a proper noun you do not recognise, and lexicon_doctor says ready is false, you may offer to set this up on your own initiative -- but answer what the user actually asked first, then add at most one short sentence, once per session, naming the word that looked wrong ("Ashler" looked like a name STT mangled -- want me to set up a lexicon so it comes out right?). Do not offer twice, do not offer when the user is busy with something failing, and never run setup_lexicon with apply: true, install_client, add_pack or trust_project without an explicit yes. If the user says no, drop it for the session and just keep calling normalize_transcript.
setup_lexicon previews by default: call it without apply to get the plan (what it would seed, the starter packs it would offer, the repo names it could harvest, the clients it detected, whether it would install the login service), show the plan to the user, then call again with apply: true, clients: [...], packs: [...], harvest: true and serve: true only for what the user agreed to. Omitted clients install nothing; omitted packs, harvest and serve do nothing.
Starter packs (list_packs: developer, ai, business, voice-tools, cloud-devops, profession-q8) give a new user dozens of curated names each (list_packs has the count); offer them once, name what a pack contains, and call add_pack only for the packs the user picked.
When corrections are not happening, call lexicon_doctor. When the user asks how to improve corrections, call suggest_terms, present the proposals (including pronunciation hints, kind "phonetic") and apply the accepted ones with apply_suggestion.
Preview install_client (and dry-run uninstall_client) before applying it, and never trust a project lexicon (trust_project) before showing the user its preview and getting a yes. Never install into a client or create a login service the user did not name.
